expertInsight: Application Architect is earned by holding four certifications, not by passing a separate exam: Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. The two architect exams are more challenging than the first two. Platform Developer I also counts toward System Architect.

whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should work toward Application Architect?

personas.label: Platform developers
personas.description: You know Apex and Lightning Web Components and want to show that you can design a full Salesforce application.

personas.label: Senior admins
personas.description: You design data models and sharing access and want to earn an architect credential.

personas.label: Solution consultants
personas.description: You design full Salesforce solutions and want a credential for architect roles.

examDifficulty.heading: Is Application Architect hard to earn?
examDifficulty.summary: There is no Application Architect exam. You earn the credential by holding Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. You must pass each exam; the two architect exams are harder than the first two.
bullets: No separate exam: You receive the credential when all four component certifications are active.
Four exams: Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect.
Separate fees and formats: Check each exam guide for current details. The App Builder and Platform Developer I exams cost less than the architect exams.
It works toward System Architect: Hold both architect credentials to apply for the Technical Architect (CTA) review board.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: A common order is Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, then Sharing and Visibility Architect. Study for each exam separately and use that exam’s practice questions.

examFormat.heading: How the Application Architect credential works
examFormat.intro: You do not book an Application Architect exam. You earn the credential by passing four separate exams:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: The two architect exams often use scenarios. They may describe a business need and ask you to choose a data model, access design, or build approach.
bestWayToPass: Start with Platform App Builder: Study declarative tools, data modeling, and automation basics.
Then take Platform Developer I: Study Apex, SOQL, triggers, and tests. This exam also counts toward System Architect.
Then take Data Architect: Study data modeling, large data volumes, master data management, and migration.
Finish with Sharing and Visibility Architect: Study org-wide defaults, role hierarchy, sharing rules, and external access.

certificationCard.description: There is no separate Application Architect exam. Earn the credential by holding Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. These practice questions cover data modeling and record access.

keyConcepts.h2: Application Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Data Modelling and Large Data Volumes
blocks.body: From the Data Architect exam: choose relationships based on how the records should work. With a **Lookup**, each record can exist on its own. With **Master-Detail**, the child depends on the parent, inherits its sharing, and can use roll-up summary fields. Deleting a parent also deletes its children. **External Objects** show data that stays in another system. **Big Objects** store very large amounts of history that is rarely changed. For large tables, keep queries **selective** by filtering on indexed fields. Watch for **data skew**, such as one parent with too many children, and plan when to archive old data.

blocks.heading: Choosing Between Configuration and Code
blocks.body: Salesforce recommends using configuration when it can meet the need. **Flow** handles most automation, including record updates, guided screens, and scheduled work. Use code when logic is complex, you need to process very large volumes, or configuration cannot do the task. Configuration is usually easier to maintain and can adapt to upgrades. Code requires tests and careful deployment, and someone must maintain it. When an answer offers a standard feature and custom code, consider the standard feature first.

blocks.heading: Designing Record Access
blocks.body: From the Sharing and Visibility exam: record access has layers, and each layer can grant more access. **Org-Wide Defaults** set the starting level; begin with the most restricted level the business needs. The **Role Hierarchy** can give managers access to their team’s records. **Sharing Rules** grant access by record owner or field values. **Teams** and **Manual Sharing** grant access to specific records. **Apex Managed Sharing** handles rules that configuration cannot express. For Experience Cloud customers, **Sharing Sets** can grant access. Profiles and Permission Sets control object and field permissions before record sharing is applied.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns for Applications
blocks.body: Use the integration pattern that fits the need. Use a synchronous callout when a user needs the answer before continuing. Use **Platform Events** or **Change Data Capture** when another system only needs to know that something changed. Use the **Bulk API** for large scheduled data loads. Use **Salesforce Connect** when data should remain in its source system. Store secrets in **Named Credentials**, not in code. Remember the limits of 100 callouts per transaction and 120 seconds total. Move slow work to asynchronous Apex so users do not have to wait.

blocks.heading: Build Quality: Testing, Deployment and Governance
blocks.body: The four exams all expect good development practices. Apex needs at least 75% test coverage for production, and tests should create their own data and check real results. Use sandboxes to build and test changes before production. Larger teams may use source control, Salesforce CLI, or DevOps Center. Design Apex for bulk processing so it works with 200 records, not just one. Track org limits and technical debt. Record why you chose a data model or access design so others can understand it later.

scenarioTips.intro: Prepare for the four component exams one at a time. These ideas appear across the exam set.

blocks.heading: Data Modelling Choices
blocks.body: Use Master-Detail when a child depends on its parent, needs roll-up summaries, or should inherit access. Use Lookup when records stand on their own. Use External Objects when data should stay in another system.

blocks.heading: Record Access Design
blocks.body: Start with the most restricted org-wide default needed. Grant more access with the role hierarchy and sharing rules. Use Apex sharing only when configuration cannot express the rule.

blocks.heading: Configuration Before Code
blocks.body: Consider Flow first. Use code when the logic is complex, the volume is large, or Flow cannot meet the need. Be ready to explain the choice.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns
blocks.body: If a user needs the response before continuing, use a synchronous callout. Use events to notify other systems. Use Bulk API for large scheduled loads. Use Salesforce Connect when data should stay in its source.

blocks.heading: Large Data Volumes
blocks.body: Keep large queries selective, avoid skewed record ownership, and plan to archive data before tables grow too large.

nextCertsAfter.heading: What to Do After Application Architect
nextCertsAfter.intro: Application Architect and System Architect together are the prerequisites for CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: An object will have 40 million records, and users need to filter by account. What should the architect plan?
options: Use selective filters with indexed fields
Copy records into nightly summary objects
Store older records in a separate Salesforce org
Block reports on the object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Large-volume queries need selective filters on indexed fields to avoid timeouts.
whyWrong: Summary copies help reporting but do not make the base object queryable.
Splitting across orgs fragments the data and complicates every query.
Blocking reporting avoids the symptom rather than solving it.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a skinny table used for?
options: Record audit history
Archive records from the main object
Validate a very large number of records
Faster reads across commonly queried fields
sampleQuestions.explanation: A skinny table stores a small set of frequently used fields so Salesforce can read them without joining standard and custom field tables.
whyWrong: Field history tracking records changes.
Archiving is a separate data lifecycle concern.
Validation is unrelated to read performance.

sampleQuestions.question: Users need read access to records they do not own based on a field value. What should the architect use?
options: Manual sharing for every record
Criteria-based Sharing Rules
Make the object public with OWD
Put all users under one role
sampleQuestions.explanation: Criteria-based Sharing Rules grant access automatically when records match field values.
whyWrong: Manual sharing does not scale and depends on owners remembering.
Making the object public grants far more access than required.
Flattening the hierarchy breaks the management visibility it provides.

sampleQuestions.question: When designing an object’s record-access model, what does the org-wide default establish before the other sharing mechanisms are applied?
options: The total number of records allowed
Which profiles can create records
Starting record access before sharing
Which fields appear on the page layout
sampleQuestions.explanation: OWD is the baseline record-access level in the model. The hierarchy and sharing rules can grant additional access, while field visibility is controlled separately.
whyWrong: There is no record cap set by the default.
Object create permission comes from the profile or permission set.
Field visibility is governed by field-level security and layouts.

sampleQuestions.question: A requirement could use Flow or Apex. What should decide which one to use?
options: How many Flows and Apex classes already exist
Which approach the team prefers
Whether configuration can meet the requirement
Whether a business or technical user requested it
sampleQuestions.explanation: Use configuration when it can meet the need. Use Apex when configuration cannot or when the requirement calls for code.
whyWrong: Existing counts say nothing about what suits this requirement.
Team preference is not an architectural criterion.
Who asked for it does not determine how it should be built.

sampleQuestions.question: What is one cost of choosing Apex when configuration could do the job?
options: Less record storage
More maintenance and testing
Higher Salesforce license fees
Loss of reporting
sampleQuestions.explanation: Apex needs tests, review, careful deployment, and ongoing maintenance.
whyWrong: Storage is unaffected by implementation choice.
Licensing does not change because logic is coded.
Reporting continues to work normally.

sampleQuestions.question: An integration must notify an outside system when an order is approved without making the user wait. What pattern fits?
options: Call the system synchronously during approval
Export approved orders in a nightly batch
Publish an event asynchronously
Ask an admin to export each order
sampleQuestions.explanation: An event can notify another system asynchronously, keeping it separate from the user’s transaction.
whyWrong: A synchronous callout makes the user wait on an external system's availability.
A nightly batch delays the notification by up to a day.
Manual export is neither timely nor reliable.

sampleQuestions.question: When should an architect choose a synchronous integration?
options: When call volume will be very high
When the outside system is slow
When the receiving system is often unavailable
When the user needs the response to continue
sampleQuestions.explanation: Use a synchronous call when the user cannot continue without a response, such as a credit check or real-time price.
whyWrong: High volume favours asynchronous handling.
A slow system is an argument against making the user wait.
Poor availability is a reason not to couple synchronously.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager needs access to records owned by their whole team. What is the simplest fit?
options: Role hierarchy with access to subordinate records
Manual sharing by each team member
A separate Sharing Rule for each manager
View All permission on the object
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Role Hierarchy can give managers access to records owned by people below them.
whyWrong: Manual sharing depends on individuals remembering every time.
Per-manager rules multiply and go stale as the organisation changes.
View All grants access to every record, far beyond the team.

sampleQuestions.question: What should an architect learn before designing record access?
options: Who must see each record and what must stay private
The number of permission sets in the org
The number of profiles from the last implementation
Which reporting tool the client will use
sampleQuestions.explanation: Start access design with the business rules for who should see which records and what must remain private.
whyWrong: Existing counts describe the present rather than the requirement.
Legacy profile counts rarely reflect what is actually needed.
Reporting tooling is downstream of the access model.

sampleQuestions.question: Why should an architect care about test coverage beyond the platform minimum?
options: It controls how many deployments can run each month
It controls whether reports can run
It increases storage
Tests help make future changes safer
sampleQuestions.explanation: Good tests help teams change the system later without breaking existing behavior.
whyWrong: Deployment frequency is not governed by coverage.
Reporting is unaffected.
Storage is unrelated to test coverage.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a Master-Detail relationship require?
options: Independent sharing for both objects
Cascade delete and inherited record access
Reparenting at any time
Only one Master-Detail relationship per object
sampleQuestions.explanation: In Master-Detail, the child depends on the parent, inherits its record access, and can be deleted with the parent.
whyWrong: The detail object inherits the master's sharing rather than having its own.
Reparenting is restricted unless explicitly allowed.
An object may have more than one master-detail relationship.

sampleQuestions.question: When is a Lookup relationship better than Master-Detail?
options: When the child must inherit access from the parent
When the child must exist without the parent
When the parent needs standard roll-up summaries
When deleting the parent must delete its children
sampleQuestions.explanation: Lookup is a better fit when the child record must be able to exist independently.
whyWrong: Inherited access is a master-detail behaviour.
Standard roll-up summaries require master-detail.
Cascade delete is a master-detail behaviour.

sampleQuestions.question: Why use a deployment pipeline with separate environments?
options: To let more admins edit production at once
To check changes before they reach production
To increase the org’s API limit
To remove the need for tests
sampleQuestions.explanation: Separate environments let a team build, test, and review a change before it reaches production.
whyWrong: Concurrent production editing is the risk a pipeline reduces.
API limits are unrelated to deployment process.
Tests remain necessary and are part of what the pipeline runs.

sampleQuestions.question: How do you earn the Application Architect credential?
options: Hold the four required certifications
Pass one scenario-based exam
Complete Trailhead superbadges and projects
Present a design to an architect panel
sampleQuestions.explanation: You earn Application Architect by holding Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. There is no separate exam.
whyWrong: There is no examination for this credential itself.
Superbadges are not what earns it.
Panel defence is part of the CTA review board, not this credential.

sampleQuestions.question: A detail record must inherit its parent’s record access and be deleted when the parent is deleted. Which relationship fits?
options: Lookup
External lookup
Indirect lookup
Master-detail
sampleQuestions.explanation: Master-detail makes the child dependent on the parent, with inherited access and cascade delete.
whyWrong: Lookup records have independent sharing.
External lookup connects to an external object.
Indirect lookup maps external data to Salesforce records.

sampleQuestions.question: A team needs to restrict field visibility for a group of users without changing their record access. Which control should it use?
options: A sharing rule
Organization-Wide Defaults
Field-level security
A role hierarchy
sampleQuestions.explanation: Field-level security controls access to fields independently of record sharing.
whyWrong: Sharing rules grant record access.
OWD sets baseline record-level access.
Role hierarchy affects record access.

sampleQuestions.question: An Apex trigger processes many records at once. Which design choice helps avoid governor-limit failures?
options: Query and update records in collections outside loops
Run one SOQL query for each record
Perform a DML statement inside each loop iteration
Use a synchronous callout for every record
sampleQuestions.explanation: Bulk processing uses collection-based queries and DML outside loops to reduce limit consumption.
whyWrong: Per-record queries can exceed SOQL limits.
Per-record DML can exceed DML limits.
Per-record callouts add latency and do not solve bulk limit usage.

sampleQuestions.question: A business process needs declarative record updates and a guided user interaction. Which platform tool should the architect assess first?
options: Apex trigger
Visualforce controller
External middleware
Flow
sampleQuestions.explanation: Flow supports declarative record automation and guided screen experiences.
whyWrong: Apex is code and may be unnecessary when Flow meets the need.
Visualforce controllers are not the default declarative option.
Middleware is unnecessary for an in-org user flow.

sampleQuestions.question: A custom object has very large data volumes and reports time out on broad queries. What should the architect evaluate first?
options: A master-detail relationship for every related object
More page layouts
Selective filters and appropriate indexed fields
A dashboard refresh schedule
sampleQuestions.explanation: Selective filters and indexes can help queries target smaller result sets at scale.
whyWrong: Relationship type alone does not solve query selectivity.
Page layouts do not affect query performance.
Refresh scheduling does not address the underlying query design.
